_: India's National Ambient Air Quality Standards beside the WHO's 2021 health-based guidelines, pollutant by pollutant and window by window. A REFERENCE TABLE, not a reading: it changes when CPCB re-notifies NAAQS or WHO revises its guidelines, and at no other time, which is why it is committed by hand and carries no fetch job. Every row pairs two figures only where BOTH bodies set one for the SAME averaging window; where one body sets none, the cell is null and the page says 'none set' rather than inventing a pairing. The two are not the same kind of thing: NAAQS is notified under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981; the WHO guideline is a recommendation with no force in Indian law.

india.name: National Ambient Air Quality Standards, 2009
india.instrument: Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part III, Section 4, No. 217, New Delhi, 18 November 2009 (notification No. B-29016/20/90/PCI-I)
india.column: Industrial, Residential, Rural and Other Area
india.compliance_note: 24 hourly or 08 hourly or 01 hourly monitored values, as applicable, shall be complied with 98% of the time in a year. 2% of the time, they may exceed the limits but not on two consecutive days of monitoring.
india.annual_note: Annual arithmetic mean of minimum 104 measurements in a year at a particular site taken twice a week 24 hourly at uniform intervals.

who.name: WHO global air quality guidelines, 2021
who.tables: Table 0.1 (recommended AQG levels) and Table 0.2 (short-averaging-time guidelines not re-evaluated in 2021, which the document says remain valid)
who.short_term_note: Table 0.1 footnote: 24-hour and 8-hour levels are the 99th percentile, i.e. 3–4 exceedance days per year. Peak-season O3 is the average of daily maximum 8-hour means in the six consecutive months with the highest six-month running average.
who.earlier_note: Rows with who_basis 'earlier' are Table 0.2 guidelines: set before 2021, not re-evaluated in the 2021 update, and stated by WHO to remain valid.
